prompt.context: Our client is a private equity firm interested in PlasticWorld, a plastic packaging manufacturer. PlasticWorld's owners are requesting $25M. The offer is final.
prompt.question: Should our client buy PlasticWorld for $25M?

clarifying_info.a: Plastic packaging for beverages, cosmetics, household and automotive chemicals. Top quality products, 350 sets of molds with different materials, finishes, and colors. Always innovating.

clarifying_info.q: Has the product mix changed recently?
clarifying_info.a: No, overall product mix has not changed in recent years.

clarifying_info.q: How is the sales force structured and compensated?
clarifying_info.a: The sales force is considered 'best in breed', they hold market share, and they are compensated based on market share.

clarifying_info.q: What can you tell me about customers?
clarifying_info.a: Customers exhibit strong loyalty. They are experiencing increasing pressures in their industries to innovate plastic packaging.

clarifying_info.q: Were there any recent capital investments?
clarifying_info.a: Two years ago they invested further in equipment for product innovation.

exhibits.title: PlasticWorld P&L Statement in the Past Three Years
exhibits.shows: A three-year P&L table (2007-2009) showing Sales, Volume, COGS, SG&A, Depreciation, and EBIT

exhibits.title: PlasticWorld and Industry Peers Profit Margins
exhibits.shows: A bar chart comparing profit margin (%) for Competitors A through F and PlasticWorld

data.axis_y: Industry Peers Profit Margins [%], range -10 to +15
data.companies: Competitor A, B, C, D, E, F (all positive margins roughly 5-12%), PlasticWorld (deeply negative, approximately -6%)

exhibits.title: PlasticWorld Valuation Sensitivity Analysis
exhibits.shows: A line chart showing company valuation ($M) as a function of profit margin (%), ranging from -10% to +15% margin and $0M to $50M valuation

data.key_points: At 0% profit margin valuation ≈ $25M; at industry average (~10%) valuation ≈ $40M

framework: 1. Current financial health: Analyze P&L to determine profit margin, revenue trends, volume trends, and cost structure
2. Competitive context: Benchmark profitability against industry peers to determine if issue is company-specific or industry-wide
3. Root cause of profitability problem: Identify why revenues are falling despite growing volume (pricing, costs, incentives)
4. Valuation: Use sensitivity analysis to determine what the company is worth and under what conditions it exceeds the $25M ask
5. Improvement levers: Identify feasible changes to bring profitability in line with industry and increase company value above $25M
6. Recommendation: Buy or no-buy decision based on value achievable post-acquisition

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 1, what observations can you make? Calculate the profit margin in 2009.
questions.guidance: Strong candidate identifies: (1) Profit margin is negative and worsening (-6% in 2009). (2) Sales volume is growing (+10.5% from 2007-2009) but revenues are falling (-4.2%), implying prices are being cut. (3) COGS is rising with volume (expected). (4) Depreciation jumped sharply from $2.25M in 2007 to $3.45M in 2008 due to equipment investment. Product mix unchanged, so the revenue decline must be a pricing issue.

math.setup: Profit margin = EBIT / Sales. For 2009: EBIT = Sales - COGS - SG&A - Depreciation
steps: Price has dropped ~13% while volume grew ~10.5%
math.answer: 2009 profit margin ≈ -6%. Revenue decline is driven by falling prices, not volume.

questions.prompt: What could be causing the price drop? What questions would you ask to investigate?
questions.guidance: Candidate should probe: (1) Is this an industry-wide pricing war? (Answer: no — request competitor data.) (2) Is the sales force incentivized to cut prices? (Answer: yes — they are compensated on market share, not profitability, giving them a direct incentive to discount.) (3) Is this driven by quality issues or customer defection? (Answer: no — customers are loyal and products are top quality.) Strongest candidates independently identify the sales force incentive misalignment as the key root cause.

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 2, what can you conclude about the profitability problem?
questions.guidance: The problem is company-specific. All six competitors show positive profit margins (roughly 5-12%), while PlasticWorld is at approximately -6%. This confirms the issue is not an industry downturn but an internal problem unique to PlasticWorld.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, what is PlasticWorld worth today, and what would it be worth at break-even and at industry average margin?
questions.guidance: At its current ~-6% margin, the company is worth well below $25M (read off the chart). At 0% margin (break-even), the valuation reaches approximately $25M — exactly the asking price. At the industry average margin (~10%), the valuation rises to approximately $40M. This means: buying at $25M is only justified if the PE firm believes it can improve margins above zero; if it can reach industry average, the upside is $15M above purchase price.

math.setup: Read from sensitivity curve in Exhibit 3
steps: Potential value creation = $40M - $25M = $15M if industry-average margins achieved
math.answer: Break-even on the deal requires reaching 0% margin; full upside to ~$40M requires reaching ~10% industry-average margin.

questions.prompt: What specific changes would you recommend to improve profitability, and how feasible are they?
questions.guidance: Two primary levers: (1) Change sales force compensation from market-share-based to earnings/profitability-based. This is easy to implement and directly removes the incentive to cut prices. (2) Simplify the product line — eliminate some of the 350 molds to reduce costs, while being mindful that customers face innovation pressures. The large mold set drives complexity and cost; pruning lower-demand SKUs reduces COGS and SG&A without necessarily losing customers given their loyalty. Also: examine industry best practices for further cost improvements.

brainstorming.prompt: What are potential ways to improve PlasticWorld's profitability post-acquisition?

categories.name: Revenue / Pricing
ideas: Raise prices — customers are loyal and quality is high, so price elasticity may be low
Reprice based on cost-plus or value-based model rather than discounting for market share
Bundle products or offer tiered pricing

categories.name: Sales Force
ideas: Shift compensation from market-share to profitability/earnings-based
Add margin hurdle to sales force incentive structure
Improve sales force training on value selling rather than discounting

categories.name: Product Line Rationalization
ideas: Eliminate low-volume molds (reduce from 350 to a leaner set)
Focus innovation investment on high-margin SKUs
Reduce complexity-driven SG&A by simplifying catalog

categories.name: Cost Structure
ideas: Review COGS for procurement or manufacturing efficiencies
Benchmark against industry peers for operational best practices
Assess whether depreciation from 2-year-old equipment investment is generating sufficient return

categories.name: Customer Strategy
ideas: Leverage customer loyalty to push through price increases
Co-develop innovation with key customers to share R&D costs

recommendation: Our client should accept the $25M offer and acquire PlasticWorld
The company is currently worth less than $25M at its -6% margin, but the acquisition is justified because the profitability problems are company-specific and fixable
With straightforward operational changes, margin can be brought to at least 0% (making the deal break-even) and potentially to industry average (~10%), implying a post-acquisition value of ~$40M
risks: Sales force resistance to compensation change may cause key performers to leave
Simplifying the product line could alienate some customers if innovation needs are not met
Execution risk: if margin improvements are slower than projected, the $25M acquisition price may not be recovered
Industry dynamics for PlasticWorld's end-customers could shift, reducing demand
next_steps: Immediately change sales force incentives from market-share to profitability-based compensation
Conduct SKU-level profitability analysis to identify which of the 350 molds to retire
Benchmark operations against industry best practices to identify further cost reduction opportunities
Monitor customer satisfaction closely during the transition to ensure loyalty is retained
